articles.title: Do trem ao VLT: Campina deve retomar transporte sobre trilhos | G1
articles.standfirst: Da rota do algodão à mobilidade urbana, relembre como funcionava a antiga ferrovia da Rainha da Borborema e conheça os planos para o VLT, que prevê 13 estações.
articles.summary: O projeto do VLT de Campina Grande prevê 13 estações e 14,8 km de trilhos, resgatando a tradição ferroviária para modernizar a mobilidade urbana da cidade.
articles.body:
VLT de Campina Grande em obras, em 2026. — Foto: Instituto Histórico de campina Grande

Os trilhos voltaram a fazer parte dos planos de transporte de Campina Grande , cidade no Agreste da Paraíba que celebra 162 anos neste domingo (11), mais de um século depois da chegada do primeiro trem à cidade, em 1907. O projeto do Veículo Leve sobre Trilhos (VLT) de Campina Grande prevê 14,8 km de extensão e 13 estações, em um percurso que inclui pontos como o Complexo Aluízio Campos, Açude Velho e áreas próximas à universidade públicas.

A proposta atual, porém, tem uma função diferente daquela exercida pela antiga ferrovia. No início do século XX, os trilhos ajudaram a mudar o comércio e a posição econômica de Campina Grande. O trem de carga continuou em atividade na cidade até o início dos anos 2000 e, depois disso, a malha ferroviária entrou em processo de sucateamento. Agora, o transporte sobre trilhos é pensado novamente para os deslocamentos dentro do próprio município .

Para entender a importância da ferrovia para a formação da segunda maior cidade da Paraíba e as diferenças entre o antigo trem e o projeto do VLT, o g1 conversou com os historiadores Erik Brito e Jefter Porto.

A ferrovia chegou a Campina Grande em 1907, em um período de valorização do algodão no mercado internacional. Até então, segundo o historiador Erik Brito, o município ainda não figurava entre as principais cidades da Paraíba. A chegada dos trilhos mudou a rota de transporte da produção do interior e aproximou Campina Grande dos mercados ligados ao porto do Recife, em Pernambuco.

Locomotiva com fardos de algodão no pátio da Estação Velha em 1949, em Campina Grande. Foto raríssima do acervo do Instituto Histórico de campina Grande — Foto: Instituto Histórico de campina Grande

Na época, os tropeiros (pessoas que transportavam mercadorias em tropas de animais) percorriam caminhos entre os sertões e o litoral para levar a produção do interior. Com a ferrovia, o algodão passou a ser levado até Campina Grande, onde era comercializado e beneficiado antes de seguir para o Recife e ser exportado.

“A chegada da malha ferroviária foi um divisor de águas para o desenvolvimento de Campina Grande. Antes de 1907, o município sequer figurava entre as potências da Paraíba. Esse evento coincidiu com a valorização do preço do algodão no mercado internacional. A ponta de trilho simbolizou o fim da necessidade dos tropeiros precisarem se deslocar dos sertões para o porto do Recife, encurtando o trajeto em quilômetros e transformando a Rainha da Borborema no principal mercado de venda e beneficiamento do algodão, fomentando uma pujança nunca antes vista na região ”, explicou Erik Brito.

O historiador Jefter Porto acrescenta que a principal finalidade da ferrovia era transportar cargas. A procura internacional por algodão crescia em meio a mudanças na produção e no consumo, ocasionada por episódios como a Guerra de Secessão nos Estados Unidos, até então o maior produtor mundial do produto, e o aumento da população e a expansão industrial no início do século XX.

Embora o transporte de cargas fosse a prioridade, o trem também levava passageiros e correspondências . O chamado Trem do Recife, por exemplo, transportava jovens da elite campinense que viajavam para estudar Direito na capital pernambucana, segundo Jefter.

“A lógica que trouxe os trilhos foi a da carga. No final da sua vida, a linha férrea passou a ser só para cargas. Mas, durante o auge, transportava passageiros e mercadorias. O beneficiamento e a distribuição do algodão, somados à condição de ponta de trilho e à localização, tornaram Campina um dos principais empórios do produto no país. Masgente também viajava. O chamado 'Trem do Recife' levava, por exemplo, jovens da elite campinense para estudar Direito na capital pernambucana”, explicou Jefter Porto.

Multidão, ameaça de cangaceiro e atraso marcaram primeira viagem do trem

Multidão aguardando chegada do primeiro trem, em Campina Grande. — Foto: Instituto Histórico de campina Grande

Cerca de 4 mil pessoas aguardavam a chegada do trem à Estação Velha de Campina Grande em 2 de outubro de 1907 . Segundo o historiador Jefter Porto, a locomotiva nº 3, da companhia inglesa Great Western, chegou enfeitada com folhas de palmeira e duas bandeiras do Brasil. A recepção teve bandas de música, girândolas e a presença de lideranças locais.

“Euforia completa. A estimativa é de que 4 mil pessoas esperavam a chegada da máquina número 3 da Great Western. Ela chegou enfeitada com folhas de palmeira e duas bandeiras do Brasil na frente. Além da curiosidade, pois muitos nunca tinham visto o trem, com relatos até de pessoas que tiveram medo do barulho ”, contou Jefter.

A expectativa pela ferrovia, no entanto, não começou naquele dia. De acordo com Jefter Porto, a chegada do trem era defendida pela elite comercial e política de Campina Grande desde a década de 1870. O historiador cita o deputado Irineu Joffily, que defendia pela instalação da linha, e o então prefeito Cristiano Lauritzen, seu adversário político. Apesar das divergências, os dois concordavam sobre a importância de levar o trem à cidade.

“A primeira viagem nutriu várias expectativas e sonhos em Campina Grande. O trem era bastante desejado pela elite comercial e política da cidade, desde a década de 1870, o Irineu Joffily já intercedia em favor do trem para a cidade. Apesar de inimigos políticos, Lauritzen e Joffily concordavam nesse ponto. Havia uma simbologia muito grande para a época, o trem para uma cidade do interior era a esperança de conexões e de expansão das redes de comércio, era o símbolo de uma cidade tida como ‘moderna’”, explicou o historiador.

A espera também ficou registrada em fotografia. O historiador Erik Brito destaca a imagem dos passageiros reunidos na Estação Velha enquanto aguardavam a chegada da composição (Veja a foto acima).

“Para nossa sorte ainda foi possível registrar uma foto do dia com os passageiros aguardando o trem na Estação Velha”, disse Erik.

No entanto, a recepção em Campina Grande contrastou com os problemas enfrentados durante a viagem. Segundo Jefter, havia rumores de que o cangaceiro Antônio Silvino e seu bando poderiam atacar a composição, mas a ameaça não se concretizou. O principal problema, de fato, foi o risco de superaquecimento da locomotiva , que precisava parar periodicamente para receber água. Em um trecho inclinado de Galante, a máquina também avançava devagar.

Estação Velha na década de 1940, em Campina Grande. — Foto: Institudo Histórico de Campina Grande

“O medo das ameaças de Antônio Silvino, que havia falado em virar o trem, que não acabou se concretizando. O grande problema era o superaquecimento da máquina que, periodicamente, tinha que parar para ser reabastecida com água. Além disso, havia o trecho de Galante que gerava receio nos passageiros da viagem inaugural, por ser um trecho inclinado, a máquina ia bastante lenta”, relatou Jefter Porto.

O historiador também recupera o relato de um jornalista enviado para cobrir a inauguração da linha. Segundo Jefter, o relato aponta que o trem saiu de Itabaiana às 15h20, já com 40 minutos de atraso, e chegou a Campina Grande por volta das 20h30. O repórter descreveu a viagem de forma negativa, criticando a falta de conforto e luxo e classificando a locomotiva como pequena e velha. Conforme o relato, a chegada ocorreu com três horas de atraso.

“Com 3 horas de atraso, o trem tão aguardado chega em Campina Grande. Apesar das expectativas locais, o jornalista do Diário de Pernambuco, mandado para cobrir a abertura da linha férrea, odiou a viagem e descreveu negativamente. Mas em Campina ninguém ligava pra isso, a euforia foi gigante ”, contou.

Trem impulsionou o comércio e a vida cotidiana

Estação Velha no ano de 1909, em Campina Grande — Foto: Instituto Histórico de campina Grande

Depois de passar a fazer parte da rotina de Campina Grande, o trem ajudou a ampliar a circulação de mercadorias pela cidade. Com a possibilidade de transportar produtos em maior quantidade, o comércio ganhou espaço e, segundo o historiador Erik Brito, o aumento desse movimento também fez mais dinheiro circular no município.

Esse crescimento contribuiu para a formação de uma burguesia regional, que passou a buscar novos serviços e espaços de convivência. De acordo com o historiador, foi nesse contexto que surgiram locais como o Cassino Eldorado e, posteriormente, o Cinema Capitólio, com serviços que antes só eram encontrados nas capitais.

“Com o grande fluxo de mercadoria, também veio um grande fluxo de dinheiro, formando uma burguesia regional. Essa elite demandava de serviços requintados o que fomentou o surgimento de espaços como o Cassino Eldorado e, posteriormente, o Cinema Capitólio, serviços que antes só eram encontrados nas capitais”, afirmou.

Esses espaços passaram a fazer parte da vida social e política da cidade. Segundo Erik Brito, as oligarquias da região se reuniam nesses locais para tomar decisões políticas e acompanhar as novidades que circulavam nas grandes cidades do mundo.

Por que o trem perdeu espaço em Campina Grande

A ferrovia que durante décadas transportou mercadorias e passageiros por Campina Grande perdeu espaço ao longo do século XX. Segundo o historiador Erik Brito, essa mudança ocorreu em diferentes partes do Brasil, em um período em que as políticas de desenvolvimento passaram a priorizar o transporte rodoviário e a expansão das estradas.

“Não só em Campina Grande, mas em todo o Brasil, o transporte ferroviário começou a perder força em meados do século XX por conta das políticas desenvolvimentistas que consideravam o trem como uma tecnologia ultrapassada. A revolução automobilística estadunidense teve muita força nesse sentido, disseminando a ideia que o futuro eram os carros. Dessa forma, a malha ferroviária brasileira entrou em um período de inércia enquanto as estradas começaram a ser abertas em larga escala em todo o país”, explicou o historiador.

Em Campina Grande, o trem de carga continuou em atividade até o início dos anos 2000. Depois, uma linha ainda foi mantida pelo projeto municipal "Trem do Forró", que fazia o percurso até o distrito de Galante durante o período junino. De acordo com Erik, porém, a falta de manutenção tornou o trajeto inviável e contribuiu para o sucateamento da malha ferroviária.

Com a interrupção dessas atividades, as antigas estruturas ligadas ao transporte sobre trilhos também passaram por um processo de deterioração. Parte dessa história, no entanto, permanece na paisagem e na memória da cidade.

“Sem manutenção, esse percurso passou a se tornar inviável, fazendo com que a malha entrasse em processo de sucateamento. As estações também entraram em processo de deterioração. Hoje, o trem não passa de uma lembrança distante de uma geração que ainda o viu em circulação, reservado apenas aos livros de história, ao Museu do Algodão, e duas instalações semi abandonadas, muito distante da representatividade que elas tiveram no século passado”, disse Erik.

Uma das construções que preservam a memória da antiga ferrovia em Campina Grande é a Estação Velha, onde funciona o Museu do Algodão. O espaço reúne objetos, documentos, fotografias e equipamentos relacionados à história da cultura algodoeira e ao desenvolvimento da cidade.

Estação Ferroviária de Campina Grande atualmente. — Foto: Reprodução / TCE-PB

O que estudo prevê para o VLT de Campina Grande

O projeto do VLT de Campina Grande prevê 14,8 quilômetros de extensão, 13 estações e quatro locomotivas . O sistema foi planejado para atender diferentes áreas do município, incluindo pontos de interesse como o Complexo Aluízio Campos, o Estádio Amigão, o Açude Velho, a Avenida Floriano Peixoto e áreas próximas à Universidade Federal de Campina Grande (UFCG) e à Universidade Estadual da Paraíba (UEPB).

As características previstas foram definidas em um Estudo de Viabilidade Técnica, Econômica e Ambiental realizado pela Prefeitura de Campina Grande, por meio das secretarias de Obras, Planejamento e Assistência Social.

O estudo estabeleceu os seguintes parâmetros para o projeto:

Extensão: 14,8 quilômetros de via permanente, ou seja, dos trilhos destinados à circulação dos trens;

Intervalo entre os trens: 17 minutos nos horários de pico. Esse intervalo é chamado de headway;

Capacidade por hora: 2.109 passageiros por sentido a cada hora;

Capacidade diária de referência: 48.408 passageiros.

A quantidade diária de passageiros foi estimada com base em diferentes percentuais de ocupação dos lugares ofertados pelo sistema. O estudo considerou três cenários:

60% de ocupação: estimativa de 29 mil passageiros por dia;

40% de ocupação: estimativa de 19,3 mil passageiros por dia;

30% de ocupação: estimativa de 14,5 mil passageiros por dia.

Em nota, a Secretaria de Planejamento afirmou que esses números são projeções do estudo de viabilidade, e não registros de passageiros transportados. A quantidade efetiva dependerá da demanda e das condições de funcionamento do sistema.

O levantamento também considerou a população que vive a até um quilômetro das estações previstas. Segundo o material da Seplan, esse público foi estimado em 47.8192 pessoas, com base nos dados populacionais de 2010.

A previsão divulgada pela Prefeitura de Campina Grande é de que as obras de infraestrutura do VLT sejam concluídas no segundo semestre de 2027.

articles.body: Saudi-led coalition fighting in Yemen has vowed a firm response to the attack on Riyadh's King Khalid International Airport, calling it a war crime. The attack killed 12 people and injured 309 others, according to Saudi authorities.According to Saudi Gazette, coalition spokesman Major General Turki Al-Maliki said the October 10 attack targeted a passenger terminal at the airport, causing civilian casualties. He blamed Yemen's Houthi militia for the strike, describing it as a violation of international humanitarian law and the customary rules of war.Al-Maliki added that the coalition's Joint Forces Command would respond firmly in accordance with international humanitarian law.The fatalities included four Saudi citizens, two Bangladeshi nationals and one national each from the United States, Egypt, Jordan, Syria, Palestine and Sudan, Saudi Gazette reported, citing the General Authority of Civil Aviation.Several of the injured remained in critical condition and were receiving treatment in hospitals. The attack also caused property damage and forced a temporary suspension of airport operations while authorities assessed the damage and checked the safety of facilities.The Houthis have not publicly claimed responsibility for the October 10 attack on Riyadh airport, despite the Saudi-led coalition blaming the group for the strike.The Iran-backed rebels have warned commercial airlines to avoid Saudi airspace, describing it as a military zone amid escalating hostilities. The warning came as Saudi Arabia intensified its military campaign against Houthi positions in Yemen, raising concerns over further attacks on civilian infrastructure and a wider regional escalation.The renewed fighting has heightened regional tensions, with Saudi Arabia stepping up military support for the Yemeni government and the Houthis continuing to pose a threat to shipping and security across the region.You use AI every day. articles.title: A Washington farmer who returned to his family farm in 1984 is challenging $618,000 in irrigation penalties after the state Supreme Court heard his case
articles.summary: A Washington farmer who returned to his family’s farm in 1984 is challenging a long-running dispute with the state Department of Ecology after penalties
articles.body: A Washington farmer who returned to his family’s farm in 1984 is challenging a long-running dispute with the state Department of Ecology after penalties over irrigation threatened the future of his agricultural business. Ron Fodé and his wife, Robin, say the agency refused to help them find a lawful way to irrigate their crops before imposing penalties that originally totalled $618,000. The case has reached the Washington Supreme Court, which heard arguments on October 1, 2026. At its centre is a question about whether the state agency followed a law requiring it to provide technical assistance to water users before moving to penalties.As reported by The Spokesman-Review, Ron and Robin Fodé wrote that the dispute had nearly destroyed their business. The couple said they once farmed 4,000 acres of owned and leased land but now lease just 290 acres. According to the Pacific Legal Foundation, the public-interest legal organisation representing Ron Fodé, the case also raises questions about whether government agencies can enforce unpublished internal policies that affect people’s legal rights.How the dispute beganRon Fodé grew up on the family farm in Grant County, Washington. He took over its operations in 1984 when his father began experiencing health problems. He and Robin raised their four children on the farm, which grew to cover about 4,000 acres at its peak. The dispute began in 2017, when Fodé needed sufficient water rights to irrigate farmland he owned and leased, including fields used to grow potatoes. Under Washington law, farmers generally need legal water rights to withdraw groundwater for irrigation. State law also allows water users to apply for seasonal transfers, which can temporarily shift water rights from one property to another.According to the Washington Court of Appeals’ 2022 ruling, Fodé applied for a seasonal change in January 2017. On February 14, a state watermaster told him that his request had been denied and that he should not irrigate the affected parcels. Fodé maintained that other water-transfer options were available and that he wanted to find a lawful way to continue watering his crops. However, according to The Spokesman-Review, the Department of Ecology refused to accept another application because he had missed an internal February 15 deadline.Fodé and his wife said the deadline had not been adopted through a public rulemaking process and that the agency had not given them access to a permitting process that could have helped them comply with the law. The Department of Ecology subsequently issued cease-and-desist orders directing Fodé and the landowners from whom he leased farmland to stop irrigating without adequate water rights.Why the penalties reached $618,000Fodé continued irrigating during the 2017 growing season. The Department of Ecology later issued penalties covering 103 days of irrigation. According to the Washington Court of Appeals’ ruling, the original penalties comprised $206,000 for irrigation on land Fodé owned, $103,000 for a 65-acre property and $309,000 for 335 acres leased from another landowner. The combined amount was $618,000. The penalties were initially issued jointly to Fodé and his landlords, but the agency later withdrew the penalties against the landlords, leaving Fodé solely liable for the amounts imposed on the three parcels.Fodé did not dispute that he lacked adequate water rights for the disputed irrigation. Instead, he argued that the penalties were invalid because the agency had failed to provide the technical assistance required by state law before imposing them. In June 2019, the Pollution Control Hearings Board upheld some of the penalties but reduced the total from $618,000 to $260,000. The dispute continued through further legal proceedings.What the farmer says the state should have doneWashington law requires the Department of Ecology to provide technical assistance to help water users identify lawful ways to comply, where applicable, before proceeding with enforcement. In their guest opinion in The Spokesman-Review, Ron and Robin Fodé argued that the agency had failed to meet that obligation. They wrote that lawmakers had recognised the complexity of the state’s water regulations and had passed a law in 2002 requiring the agency to provide technical assistance before imposing penalties. According to the couple, the agency should have helped them identify a lawful water-transfer option rather than rejecting their application because of an internal deadline.Their opinion also quoted a regional water resources programme manager at the Department of Ecology as saying, “That’s just something we didn’t do,” when asked why the agency had not provided the assistance they said the law required. The Fodés argue that the February 15 deadline effectively blocked them from applying for a seasonal transfer, even though it had not been formally adopted through a public process. They say the case is therefore about more than the penalties against their farm: it concerns whether agencies can impose rules affecting the public without following the required legal procedures. The Department of Ecology’s position and the legal questions must be assessed through the court proceedings; the couple’s guest opinion presents their account of the dispute.What the courts have ruled so farThe Washington Court of Appeals addressed part of the dispute in a ruling dated May 12, 2022. It held that Fodé’s appeals against the cease-and-desist orders were timely under the relevant statutory definition of when an agency decision is received. The court also reversed a later trial-court order that had sent the appeals concerning the cease-and-desist orders back to the administrative board. It said the proper route was to remand the penalty appeal so that technical-assistance evidence that had been wrongly excluded could be considered. That ruling did not resolve the entire dispute over the penalties. The case subsequently moved to the Washington Supreme Court, which agreed to review the matter in June 2026. The Pacific Legal Foundation says the Supreme Court case concerns whether the Department of Ecology must comply with the legislature’s limits on its enforcement authority. The organisation is representing Fodé without charge. The Supreme Court heard arguments on October 1.A family farm reduced to 290 acresThe prolonged dispute has had a substantial effect on the family’s agricultural operation. The Fodés said they have had to sell nearly everything they once farmed, reducing their operation from 4,000 acres of owned and leased land to 290 leased acres. They argue that the conflict could have been avoided if the agency had helped them identify a lawful route to irrigation before imposing penalties. The court’s decision will determine the legal questions before it. Until then, the dispute remains unresolved, and the Fodés continue to challenge the state’s handling of their irrigation application and the penalties that followed.You use AI every day. articles.title: 'Starlink poses risk to security agencies': BJP MP Nishikant Dubey responds to Musk's charge
articles.summary: NEW DELHI: BJP MP Nishikant Dubey on Sunday hit back at SpaceX CEO Elon Musk amid the dispute over Starlink’s entry into India, alleging that the
articles.body: NEW DELHI: BJP MP Nishikant Dubey on Sunday hit back at SpaceX CEO Elon Musk amid the dispute over Starlink’s entry into India, alleging that the satellite internet service poses challenges to the country’s security agencies and asserting that India would not change its security policy under pressure.In a post on X, Dubey, chairman of a parliamentary committee, said the panel had examined the challenges faced by country's security agencies in connection with Starlink.“The ministry of defence, the ministry of home affairs, and our investigation agencies are being affected by the dangerous games of these threats,” Dubey wrote.He also claimed that the government led by former prime minister Manmohan Singh had alerted the Telecom Regulatory Authority of India (TRAI) to such threats in 2013-14.Urging Musk to focus on making internet services affordable in the United States before criticising India, Dubey said the country was a sovereign democracy and would not alter its security policy in response to pressure or social media posts.“First, provide connections to the poor in your own country, America, at affordable rates, and then level accusations—India is a healthy democratic, sovereign nation; it does not change its security policy under pressure or social media,” he said.Dubey added that if financial considerations alone determined the government's decisions, it would have welcomed Starlink despite objections from security agencies.“If our policy were driven by money, we would have rolled out the red carpet welcome for you despite opposition from the security agencies,” he wrote.Musk's allegations over Starlink's India entryDubey's remarks came after Musk argued that Starlink's entry would increase competition and give Indian consumers more choices.SpaceX chief criticised what he described as arguments by supporters of Reliance Industries chairman Mukesh Ambani against the satellite internet service.“The reality is that competition would greatly benefit the average citizen in India by giving them more choices, as it always does. Ambani’s profits will be lower, but he is not going out of business,” Musk wrote.The exchange follows Musk's earlier allegations that influential business groups were obstructing Starlink's entry to protect their market positions. He had also addressed Ambani as “Prime Minister Ambani” and accused him of seeking to preserve a monopoly.The government has rejected the suggestion that Starlink is being singled out, saying commercial operations depend on regulatory and security clearances.At the India Mobile Congress 2026 in New Delhi, Union communications minister Jyotiraditya Scindia said India would not allow a monopoly in any sector.Starlink, Reliance Jio Satcom and Bharti Airtel-backed Eutelsat OneWeb have received licences, but the government has said security clearances remain pending for the operators. The satellite spectrum pricing framework is also being finalised.Get the latest India News and Live updates. Download the TOI app.

articles.title: A 70-year-old woman swam 20 miles across California's Catalina Channel after her brother received a kidney transplant; she raised over €15,000
articles.summary: Maura Twomey, a 70-year-old former primary school teacher who lives in Boston, crossed California's Catalina Channel on 17 August in an unofficial time of
articles.body: Maura Twomey, a 70-year-old former primary school teacher who lives in Boston, crossed California's Catalina Channel on 17 August in an unofficial time of 15 hours, 45 minutes and 23 seconds, pending ratification. She became the oldest person to complete the crossing and earned the Triple Crown of Open Water Swimming. She swam in honour of her youngest brother, Martin, who received a kidney from a deceased donor in June after two and a half years on dialysis. Her fundraising page shows €17,022 raised online for the IKA against a target of €15,000.How did the 70-year-old woman swim Catalina ChannelAccording to the Irish Kidney Association, Maura Twomey is a native of Ireland who lives in Boston and finished the Catalina Channel crossing on 17 August in an unofficial time of 15:45:23, pending ratification. The swim made her the oldest person to complete the crossing, and it also earned her the Triple Crown of Open Water Swimming, which consists of the English Channel, the 20 Bridges Swim and the Catalina Channel.Her open-water career began with a swim from Alcatraz around her 50th birthday. She then completed the English Channel in 2015, swimming from England to France in 16 hours and 23 minutes at the age of 59. She followed this eight years later with the 20 Bridges Swim around Manhattan in 9 hours and 19 minutes.Why did Martin Twomey need a kidney transplantMartin Twomey, now 60, is the youngest of 14 siblings, and Maura is the seventh eldest. He was born in Dublin, spent his early years in Walkinstown, and moved with his family to Blarney, Co. Cork, when he was five. He now lives in Douglas, Co. Cork, close to his four adult sons, Darren, Daniel, Conor and Liam, and his two grandchildren, Beth (13) and Harry (16). He had built a transport business with a fleet of 30 buses and stepped back from it last year because he was no longer well enough to run it.Martin's wife, Catherine, died from a brain aneurysm in 2023, and he agreed to donate her organs and heart valves. Six months later, his kidney function had deteriorated to the point where he needed to start haemodialysis. He spent two and a half years on dialysis at Cork University Hospital before receiving a kidney from a deceased donor in June this year. The transplant took place at Beaumont Hospital.Several family members, including Maura, offered to donate a kidney as living donors, but Martin declined. He was concerned that a donor might one day need their remaining kidney, or that another family member might need it. Maura Twomey is quoted by the IKA as saying: "Martin always put the welfare of his family before his own."How difficult was Maura’s Catalina Channel swimMaura described the swim as every bit as demanding as she had expected. She said: "The swim began in 12-knot winds, chop and swells that never completely settled." She added that in the final hours the winds rose to approximately 20 knots, pushing her off course. She said that whenever she felt she had nothing left, she thought of Martin and what he had endured on dialysis.She made the crossing aboard the Kamryn Dawson, supported by crew chief Elaine Howley and crew member and support swimmer Barbara Cocci. Kayak support was provided by Sidney Russell and Angela Lee, while David Sundius and Joel Virgil served as official observers for the Catalina Channel Swimming Federation. Reaching land meant scrambling up a rocky shoreline to complete the swim, which left her with a skinned knee. She credits Cork-based swim coach Eilis Burns, whom she approached in 2015 when she set out to swim the English Channel.How much did Maura raise for the Irish Kidney AssociationMaura chose to fundraise for Irish Kidney Association CLG, and all funds raised there go directly to the cause. The page records a total of €17,022 raised against a target of €15,000, all of it from online donations. It lists the fundraiser as completed, with donations available until 4 September 2026. The top donors shown are Martin Twomey with €1,000, Mr O'Connor with €502 and Derry Cronin with €500.IKA is working to meet the needs of people and their families living with and affected by end-stage kidney disease, on dialysis and post-transplant. It states that funds from donations and fundraisers provide services such as counselling, financial aid, the use of a patient support centre and patient holidays. articles.title: Meet T’Emi Oshin, the 20-year-old Wayne State student who scored 1590 on the SAT and became the university’s first Obama-Chesky Voyager Scholar; she is also being honoured for youth advocacy and public-health work
articles.summary: For T’Emi Oshin, medicine was never simply about what happens inside a clinic. Long before college, the Midland native imagined herself becoming a doctor.
articles.body: For T’Emi Oshin, medicine was never simply about what happens inside a clinic. Long before college, the Midland native imagined herself becoming a doctor. But as she grew older, science, public health and community work broadened that ambition, showing her that improving lives can begin well before a patient reaches an examination room. At 20, Oshin is now a junior at Wayne State University, studying public health and neuroscience while preparing for medical school, states an online report by Midland Daily News. Alongside her academic journey, she has built a record of youth advocacy and community leadership that has recently earned her two significant honours. Scroll down to read about her journey.A first for Wayne StateIn September, Oshin was selected for the 2026-28 class of Obama-Chesky Voyager Scholars, becoming the first student from Wayne State University to receive the public service scholarship, states the online report.The programme offers financial support, mentorship and funding for a summer work experience that scholars design themselves. Oshin plans to use the opportunity in 2027 to learn from youth-led organisations in other communities, exploring how young people are tackling challenges around them and what barriers they face.The scholarship comes at a point when Oshin is increasingly interested in the space between medicine and public policy. She hopes to become a physician, with primary care and paediatrics among the areas she is considering, but she is also curious about the role of nonprofits and government in creating healthier communities, adds the report.Finding her voice through communityAs per the report, Oshin's commitment to advocacy began during her school years in Midland. As a junior at H.H. Dow High School, she founded the Black Student Alliance after conversations with fellow Black students revealed a need for greater connection and a safe space to discuss their experiences.The initiative grew beyond simply creating a community for students. Members gave presentations to younger students about Black history and related subjects, turning the group into a platform for education and engagement. Oshin later helped establish Black Youth of Midland, bringing young people from different schools together for monthly meetings at the Midland Area Community Foundation. Her introduction to philanthropy also came through the foundation's Midland Area Youth Action Council. The experience helped shape an interest that has since become an important part of her work.Academic excellence with a wider purposeOshin's academic record has been equally striking. She graduated from Dow High in 2024 and was named one of 625 semifinalists in the U.S. Presidential Scholars Program, selected from more than 6,000 candidates nationwide. She also earned a 1590 on the SAT, one of the highest scores associated with Dow High. At Wayne State, she is part of the BS/MD Med-Direct programme, combining undergraduate education with a pathway toward medical school, adds the online report.Her interest in public health developed during high school as she became more aware of how factors outside a doctor's office can influence health outcomes. That perspective has particularly drawn her toward Black youth mental health and the broader conditions that shape young people's wellbeing.A new chapter in public serviceOshin's growing list of accomplishments has now added another distinction. On November 18, she is scheduled to receive the Outstanding Young Philanthropist award at the National Philanthropy Day Awards Luncheon at Saginaw Valley State University. The Midland Area Community Foundation nominated her for the honour.Behind the awards is a network of teachers and mentors who helped nurture her interests, from science educators and STEM mentors to advisers who supported her youth advocacy efforts.For Oshin, the next chapter appears to be less about collecting achievements and more about understanding how those achievements can translate into service. Whether that eventually takes her into a clinic, a nonprofit, government or a combination of all three, her goal remains rooted in the same idea that shaped her ambitions as a child: using knowledge to make life better for others.Images Courtesy: Midland Daily NewsYou use AI every day. articles.summary: Dramatic videos from Nepal show the scale of destruction caused by a flash flood along the Budhi Gandaki River in Gorkha district, with entire sections of
articles.body: Dramatic videos from Nepal show the scale of destruction caused by a flash flood along the Budhi Gandaki River in Gorkha district, with entire sections of settlements swept away, bridges destroyed and homes reduced to debris.Visuals from the affected region show floodwaters tearing through Salleri Bazaar, causing severe damage in Jagat Bazaar and sweeping away the Soti Khola Bridge.A short while ago: A devastating flash flood has swept away Salleri Bazaar (Market) and caused severe destruction in Jagat Bazaar along the Budhi Gandaki River, Gorkha District, Nepal.(Video provided by Umesh.) Weather Monitor (@WeatherMonitors) October 11, 2026Other footage shows homes, buildings and bridges being carried away by the powerful, debris-laden waters.At least 10 people have been reported missing since Sunday morning after the sudden surge in the Budhi Gandaki River basin, according to officials cited by news agency ANI.However, the full extent of the damage remains unclear.Homes, bridges swept away as floodwaters surgeThe flooding has devastated settlements in the northern part of Gorkha district, including Salleri, Jagat, Dovan and Ghattekhola. Preliminary reports suggest that around 35 houses were swept away in Painyu and Bagar in Ward 3 of Chumnubri Rural Municipality.The disaster has also destroyed or damaged six bridges, including motorable bridges and suspension bridges, disrupting connections between several settlements.Bridges at Arughat, Tripurasundari and Soti-Manbu were among those swept away, assistant chief district officer Netra Prasad Sharma told ANI. A Bailey bridge linking wards 1 and 3 of Dharche Rural Municipality was also destroyed.The flood had damaged a hydropower project in the district. Authorities have yet to establish the cause of the sudden surge, while residents have raised the possibility that a blocked tributary or a landslide may have triggered the flooding.Army, helicopters deployed for rescue operationsNepal has mobilised security personnel and helicopters to evacuate residents and provide relief in the affected region.Prime Minister Balendra Shah said a Nepali Army contingent had been deployed by air and land for search and rescue operations. A rapid response team from Kathmandu was also airlifted to the area.The Nepal Army subsequently said six people had been evacuated to safer locations, ANI reported.Home minister Sudan Gurung urged people living along the Budhi Gandaki River to move to safer areas, warning that the river's flow continued to fluctuate.Police, the Armed Police Force and local authorities have been mobilised for rescue and evacuation efforts.The National Disaster Risk Reduction and Management Authority has also urged residents in vulnerable riverside settlements to relocate and remain alert, according to AP.The cause of the flash flood remains under investigation.The disaster comes as Nepal continues to grapple with the aftermath of the Bhotekoshi-Trishuli floods on August 26, which resulted in the deaths of 1,455 people and left 5,285 missing.The tragedy also caused significant damage to homes and infrastructure, leaving communities in mountainous areas vulnerable to further disruption.You use AI every day. articles.title: From peaceful protests to free movement: 9 directions SC issued amid CJP stir in Delhi
articles.summary: NEW DELHI: The Supreme Court on Sunday stepped into the row over restrictions imposed during the Cockroach Janta Party's (CJP) protest in Delhi, directing
articles.body: NEW DELHI: The Supreme Court on Sunday stepped into the row over restrictions imposed during the Cockroach Janta Party's (CJP) protest in Delhi, directing authorities to prevent illegal detentions, ensure normal Metro and railway operations and protect the ability of lawyers and journalists to perform their duties. The court also ordered the removal of a notice board announcing prohibitory restrictions near its premises, saying citizens and lawyers must have access to justice.A bench of Justices Joymalya Bagchi and V Mohana issued notice to the Centre on a contempt plea alleging that authorities had violated the court's October 9 directions on public transport restrictions. The hearing came a day after more than 7,000 people were detained during a security crackdown on the planned mobilisation at Jantar Mantar against Chief Election Commissioner Gyanesh Kumar.During the special sitting, lawyers alleged that detentions and movement restrictions had extended beyond the areas covered by prohibitory orders. Solicitor General Tushar Mehta, however, told the court that restrictions on October 10 covered 45 of Delhi Metro's 303 stations and that most detainees had already been released.Here are the key actions and directions from the Supreme Court hearing.Authorities told to prevent illegal detentionsThe court made clear that people assembling peacefully cannot be detained outside the bounds of the law, particularly in areas not covered by prohibitory orders under Section 163 of the Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita (BNSS)."There shall not be illegal detention, save and except by procedure established by law, particularly with regard to assemblage of people beyond the area within which it's imposed," the bench said.The issue was raised by senior advocate Kapil Sibal, appearing for RJD MP Manoj Jha. Sibal alleged that police were detaining people travelling by train and individuals outside the four-kilometre radius of Jantar Mantar, where prohibitory orders were in force.Normal Metro and railway operations to be ensuredThe Supreme Court directed that Delhi Metro services should operate according to their normal schedule and asked Solicitor General Tushar Mehta, appearing for the Centre, to ensure that the authorities concerned complied with the direction. It also called for railway services to function without a blanket prohibition, subject to lawful and necessary restrictions.The direction followed the court's October 9 order, passed after a separate petition challenged the closure of 57 Metro stations and cancellation of trains in view of the planned protest.On Sunday, Mehta said entry and exit had been restricted at 45 of the network's 303 stations on October 10, accounting for around 15 per cent of the total. Lawyers appearing before the court had alleged that the restrictions continued despite the earlier order, with some stations completely inaccessible to passengers. Internet access must not be disrupted unlawfullyThe bench directed the authorities to ensure that internet services remained undisturbed, subject to law and order requirements. It also clarified that the direction did not curtail powers available under the Information Technology Act."Internet facilities shall remain undisturbed, as per law....When we are saying internet facilities shall remain undisturbed, we are not taking away the powers under the Information Technology Act," the bench said.The court's observation sought to ensure that restrictions imposed amid the security operation did not extend to internet connectivity without lawful justification.Free movementThe court called for free movement of people, subject to traffic regulations, and for authorities to review the need for barricades that could impede movement across Delhi.Senior advocate Gopal Sankaranarayanan urged the bench to direct the removal of barricades and restoration of services at Metro stations. Lawyers had argued that restrictions were affecting not only protesters but also other residents and commuters.The court's broader directions sought to ensure that security measures did not impose unnecessary hardship on people moving around the capital.Lawyers, journalists must be allowed to workThe bench directed authorities to ensure that lawyers, journalists and others were not obstructed from discharging their professional duties.The direction came amid allegations that several lawyers had been detained during Saturday's protests. Senior advocate Shadan Farasat, who said he was detained by Delhi Police, told the court that he and other lawyers had faced violence."It's about citizens' right to protest. The sense I got yesterday was that we were one step away from a police state. Kindly restore citizens' right to protest peacefully in the capital. Yesterday, that right was destroyed," Farasat said.Senior advocate Gopal Sankaranarayanan also informed the bench that senior advocates Dinesh Dwivedi, Uttara Babbar and Farasat had been detained.Section 163 notice board near SC ordered to be removedThe court directed the concerned authority to take down a notice board announcing the imposition of Section 163 of the BNSS in and around the Supreme Court premises, if it had not already been removed."We have been informed that a notice board stating imposition of Section 163 BNSS in and around the vicinity of the Supreme Court has been put up," the bench said."We direct the authority concerned to take down this board, if not already done, so that citizens as well as lawyers can have access to justice," it ordered.The direction was specifically linked to ensuring access to the court for citizens and members of the legal profession.Peaceful protests permitted, but must remain within the lawThe bench observed that peaceful assemblies must be allowed in accordance with law, particularly outside areas where prohibitory orders apply. It also reminded protesters that demonstrations must remain peaceful and should not instigate others.The hearing centred on the distinction between lawful regulation to maintain public order and restrictions that effectively prevent people from exercising their rights.In its October 9 order, the Supreme Court had said authorities could regulate Metro and railway operations but should not impose an outright prohibition on their movement. It had also asked the government to publicise transport arrangements and issue traffic advisories to minimise inconvenience.Habeas corpus and related pleas listed for October 13The court said petitions concerning alleged mass detentions and other connected matters would be heard alongside the main cases on October 13.One of these was a habeas corpus petition filed by senior advocate Menaka Guruswamy concerning the detention of political leaders. The bench was also hearing Jha's plea alleging disproportionate use of force, illegal detention, house arrests and harassment of protesters by Delhi Police.The allegations in Jha's petition included claims of sexual harassment of women protesters. These were allegations before the court and had not been established by the directions issued on Sunday.Centre issued notice in contempt pleaThe bench issued notice to the Centre on a contempt petition filed by advocate Shailendra Mani Tripathi, which named Union home secretary Govind Mohan, Delhi Police Commissioner Anurag Kumar and Delhi Metro Rail Corporation chairperson D Thara as respondents.The petition alleged that authorities had breached the Supreme Court's October 9 order by restricting public transport and detaining protesters on October 10.The earlier order had followed a plea challenging the closure of Metro stations and cancellation of trains ahead of the CJP mobilisation. The court had observed that notifications appeared to go beyond regulation and impose a complete ban on essential public transport.The bench had said: "Upon our indication that a distinction exists between total 'prohibition' and the 'regulation' of metro and other train movements, the solicitor general of India has fairly agreed to impress upon the authorities to reassess such prohibitions."The court's latest intervention came as it considered allegations that the earlier directions had not been followed. It also reiterated its responsibility under Article 32 of the Constitution to protect and enforce fundamental rights.Get the latest India News and Live updates. Download the TOI app.

articles.title: A New Zealand man spent 11 years building a 370-metre miniature railway around his Whanganui home, with 10 tunnels, two bridges and two stations; the property has now sold for NZ$240,000 to a family keeping the railway
articles.summary: Some home improvements are measured in fresh paint, landscaped gardens or a new kitchen. Ian Jones took a rather different approach.
articles.body: Some home improvements are measured in fresh paint, landscaped gardens or a new kitchen. Ian Jones took a rather different approach. Over 11 years, the New Zealand retiree transformed his Whanganui property into a miniature railway world, complete with tunnels, bridges, stations and enough track to turn an ordinary residential section into a tiny transport network. Now, after years of building and tinkering, the property on Cornfoot Street in Castlecliff has a new owner. Sold for NZ$240,000, the home will remain connected to its most unusual feature, with the family buying it planning to keep the railway, states an online report by TradeMe.From online find to backyard railwayThe project began almost casually. Jones, who owns several properties in Whanganui, came across a child-sized petrol locomotive being sold online and decided to buy it. That small purchase eventually became the Nikau Junction Railway, a 370-metre miniature track winding through the property. What started as a whim grew steadily, with Jones adding 10 tunnels, two bridges, an artificial hill and two stations, adds the online report.The complete circuit takes around 12 minutes to travel, with the track arranged in two interconnected loops. For visitors, the railway was more than an ornamental feature. It was a functioning ride built over years of hands-on work, the online report claims. The unusual property attracted national attention when it was listed earlier this year, with photographs putting the miniature railway front and centre.A buyer willing to keep the trainsFinding someone who wanted both the property and its railway was never guaranteed. The listing generated considerable interest, but many prospective buyers were primarily interested in the land and viewed the elaborate railway as less important.Eventually, the right match emerged. The new owners, a couple with a teenager, already have an unconventional living arrangement and plan to continue using the property in much the same spirit. They currently live in a bus and intend to sell it before moving the bus onto the Castlecliff property. The family also plans to retain the miniature railway, ensuring that Jones's 11-year project will continue under new ownership, adds the online report.The sale price of NZ$240,000 was NZ$20,000 above the property's rateable value, a notable result in a market where some vacant sections have struggled to find buyers, the report mentions.One railway, several chaptersFor Jones, selling the property does not mean abandoning miniature railways. At 70, the retiree is already turning his attention to other interests, including renovating his own home, which had been neglected while much of his time went into the railway project.He will also remain involved in trains through a friend's much larger model railway project near Castlecliff. The property is being developed into a wedding venue, giving Jones another opportunity to indulge his hobby without having to own the railway himself. During the sales process, prospective buyers could view the property by appointment. Some were even taken for rides, turning a conventional property inspection into something closer to a small attraction.A quirky property finds its peopleThe Castlecliff home may have started as an ordinary residential property, but 11 years of work gave it a personality few listings can match. Its tunnels, bridges, stations and winding track transformed a piece of land into a miniature world. Now the railway has found owners who intend to keep it running. For Jones, the project moves into its next chapter, while the new family gets something considerably more unusual than a house: a home with its own railway network in the backyard.Images Courtesy: TradeMeReady to Make a Smarter Property Decision? articles.title: Putin tells Trump Russia will fight until ‘all objectives’ are met, rules out Ukraine war peace breakthrough
articles.summary: Russian President Vladimir Putin has ruled out an immediate end to the war in Ukraine, telling US President Donald Trump that Moscow would continue
articles.body: Russian President Vladimir Putin has ruled out an immediate end to the war in Ukraine, telling US President Donald Trump that Moscow would continue fighting until it achieved all its objectives. The phone call came hours before Russian strikes killed at least 20 people, including three children, in Ukraine on Saturday.According to the New York Post (NYP), Putin made the remarks during a 90-minute conversation with Trump on Friday. Russian foreign policy aide Yuri Ushakov said Moscow would continue military operations until it achieved its stated goals.“Putin made it clear that Moscow will continue hostilities until it achieves all stated goals,” Ushakov told Russian state media.Putin also reportedly sought to convince Trump that Ukraine had no prospects of winning the war and that Russia had the outcome entirely in its hands. However, recent battlefield developments have included Ukrainian forces reclaiming territory, challenging Moscow's claims of having the upper hand.Ushakov said Trump had agreed to convey Putin's message about the prospects for peace talks to the Ukrainian government. The two leaders reportedly continued their conversation for an extended period, with neither wanting to end the call first.The conversation followed six hours of high-level discussions organised by the United States on Friday. The meeting included US special envoy Steve Witkoff, Ukrainian negotiators and representatives from the United Kingdom, France, Germany, the European Commission and NATO. However, the talks failed to produce a breakthrough.The diplomatic developments have also strained relations between Washington and Kyiv. Ukrainian officials said they were caught off guard by the Trump administration's decision to ease export sanctions on Russia, allowing Russian diesel fuel to be shipped to the United States.Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky criticised the move as a “weak decision”, arguing that it could help sustain Russia's war effort. A senior Ukrainian official described the development as feeling like a trap, according to the Kyiv Independent.Hours after the Trump-Putin conversation, Russian forces struck a residential neighbourhood in Zaporizhzhia with five guided aerial bombs early Saturday, killing at least 20 people and injuring 18, Ukraine's State Emergency Service said.Three children, including an 11-year-old boy, were among those killed. Emergency workers searched through the rubble for survivors and victims, with some people reportedly trapped for several hours.Mykhailo Semikin, acting governor of Zaporizhzhia, expressed grief over the deaths, saying the children should have had the chance to grow up, pursue their dreams and learn about the world.“There are no words that can ease the pain of families who have lost their loved ones,” he said in a message on Telegram.The latest strikes came amid continued uncertainty over diplomatic efforts to end the war, with Putin signalling that Russia would press ahead with its military campaign and US-led talks failing to deliver an immediate path towards peace.You use AI every day. More than 7,000 protesters were detained, including CJP leader Abhijit Dipke, several opposition leaders and YouTuber Dhruv Rathee.During the special hearing, the bench asked Solicitor General Tushar Mehta to ensure that Delhi Metro operates according to its regular schedule and that internet services are not disrupted, subject to law and order requirements.The court also directed authorities to ensure that lawyers, journalists and others are not prevented from carrying out their professional duties."Internet facilities shall remain undisturbed, as per law....When we are saying internet facilities shall remain undisturbed, we are not taking away the powers under the Information Technology Act."There shall not be illegal detention, save and except by procedure established by law, particularly with regard to assemblage of people beyond the area within which it's imposed," the bench said.The Supreme Court also directed authorities to remove a notice board outside its premises announcing the imposition of Section 163 of the Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita (BNSS), which empowers authorities to restrict assemblies in certain circumstances."We have been informed that a notice board stating imposition of Section 163 BNSS in and around the vicinity of the Supreme Court has been put up."We direct the authority concerned to take down this board, if not already done, so that citizens as well as lawyers can have access to justice," the bench ordered.During the hearing, senior advocate Kapil Sibal, appearing for Rashtriya Janata Dal (RJD) MP Manoj Jha, alleged that police were detaining people travelling on trains and those found outside the four-kilometre radius of Jantar Mantar, where prohibitory orders were in force.Sibal also told the court that 45 metro stations had remained closed to passenger entry and exit despite the Supreme Court's October 9 order.The petition sought contempt proceedings against the authorities over the alleged failure to comply with the court's directions on maintaining access to public transport during the protests.Get the latest India News and Live updates. articles.title: Mark Zuckerberg’s Gothic castle in Ireland costs more than previously thought; he paid $56 million for the main house alone and the full 440-acre price remains ‘secret’
articles.summary: Mark Zuckerberg and his wife, Priscilla Chan, have paid significantly more – almost double – for their historic Irish castle than initial market estimates
articles.body: Mark Zuckerberg and his wife, Priscilla Chan, have paid significantly more – almost double – for their historic Irish castle than initial market estimates suggested, spending over €51 million (approximately $56 million) on the central residence alone, a report by The Irish Times said, citing official property records. According to data published by Ireland’s official Property Price Register, the transaction for Strancally Castle in County Waterford finalised at €51,171,155. The recorded figure is roughly double the price real estate insiders projected when news of the deal first emerged, with early estimates placing the sale between €20 million and €30 million.The real cost behind the 440-acre estateWhile the register records a €51.17 million sum, that figure accounts strictly for the principal residential castle and up to one acre of surrounding land. As the historical property spans a massive 440-acre riverside estate, the total expenditure incurred by the couple remains undisclosed on the residential registry and is expected to substantially exceed the registered amount once the full acreage and surrounding grounds are factored in, the report said.The transaction was formally dated on August 17, 2026, just three days before local reporting in The Irish Times first disclosed the purchase.History and scale of Strancally CastlePositioned on the banks of the River Blackwater, Strancally Castle is an architectural landmark constructed in the Gothic-revival style. It was built around 1830 for former Tory MP John Keily, and the property was envisioned by prominent architect brothers James and George Richard Pain, who also designed a nearby folly tower house and an inlet quay along the river.According to the historical book The Houses of Ireland by Brian De Breffny and Rosemary Ffolliott, the three-storey estate encompasses 16,000 square feet, laid out on such an expansive floor plan that it required “a brisk walk of 4 and half minutes to reach the dining room from the kitchen.”The estate was acquired 25 years ago by Michael Alen-Buckley, co-founder of London investment firm RAB Capital, and his wife, Giancarla Alen-Buckley, the daughter of late hotelier Charles Forte and sister to Rocco Forte Hotels chairman Rocco Forte. Over the past two decades, the couple oversaw a comprehensive restoration of the property.In a departure statement, the Alen-Buckleys noted:“We leave our home of 25 years fondly and are grateful for the opportunity we have been given to save and restore Strancally Castle … We are delighted that Mark and his family intend to build on our stewardship by continuing to invest in maintaining and enhancing the property and grounds as their home in a sustainable manner … We wish them and their family much happiness in this unique and blessed place.”Meta’s Irish footprint and personal tiesZuckerberg’s search for prime real estate in Ireland first surfaced publicly last summer, after Liberty Media owner John Malone told The Wall Street Journal that the tech executive had approached him with an offer to buy his Castlemartin House and Estate in County Kildare. While Zuckerberg and Chan will maintain their permanent home in the US, they plan to use Strancally Castle as a family residence when visiting Ireland.Moreover, the property gives the Meta founder a direct base near his company's key international operations. Meta, parent company of Facebook and Instagram, has operated its European headquarters out of Ireland since 2009, where it currently employs roughly 1,500 people.You use AI every day. articles.title: ‘No place to breathe’: AISA’s Neha Bora detained again, alleges police brutality
articles.summary: NEW DELHI: AISA president Neha Bora was detained again on Sunday during protests demanding the resignation of Chief Election Commissioner Gyanesh Kumar,
articles.body: NEW DELHI: AISA president Neha Bora was detained again on Sunday during protests demanding the resignation of Chief Election Commissioner Gyanesh Kumar, and alleged that Delhi Police were using detention buses with separate cells to hold demonstrators in cramped conditions.In a video shared on social media, Bora claimed that the buses had four “cells” and alleged that there was barely any room to breathe inside them. She also accused police personnel of abusing and kicking male protesters.“This is the bus. The bus has 4 ‘cells’, There is no place to breath,” Bora said, alleging that the detention facilities were being used like jails. “Are detention buses being turned into jail? CRPF is waging war against common people of the country. Why so much violence just because you want to protect Gyanesh Kumar?” she added.Bora was detained along with other protesters near Vijay Chowk as demonstrators attempted to march towards Jantar Mantar amid heavy security deployment across the capital.Visuals showed the AISA president raising slogans alongside other members before protesters ran as security personnel moved in to stop them. Several demonstrators were subsequently taken into custody.More than 100 protesters were detained at various locations across Delhi on Sunday as members of student organisations, including the Students' Federation of India (SFI), AISA and Krantikari Yuva Sangathan (KYS), joined the protest called by the Cockroach Janata Party (CJP).CPI(M) Rajya Sabha MP John Brittas was also among those detained, according to police sources.The SFI alleged that its activists had been assaulted inside cage-like police vans. It also claimed that Brittas was attacked by police personnel and later left by the roadside in an injured condition. The organisation further alleged that Father Biju Xavier, vicar of Sacred Heart Church in Delhi, was detained while recording alleged police violence.The detentions came amid extensive security arrangements, with more than 30,000 police and paramilitary personnel deployed across Delhi to prevent protesters from reaching Jantar Mantar.The CJP and opposition parties have been demanding Kumar's resignation over alleged irregularities in the functioning of the Election Commission and the Special Intensive Revision (SIR) of electoral rolls.Get the latest India News and Live updates. articles.title: In Colorado, a family spent more than 60 years assembling a working ranch; after it was once listed for $100 million, Susan Nottingham has now permanently protected 18,484 acres and their historic water rights
articles.summary: A nearly 20,000-acre cattle ranch in Colorado, United States, which was once put up for sale for $100 million, has now been permanently protected from
articles.body: A nearly 20,000-acre cattle ranch in Colorado, United States, which was once put up for sale for $100 million, has now been permanently protected from development. Its owner, Susan Nottingham, has worked with conservation organisations to preserve 18,484 acres of the Nottingham Ranch, along with its historic water rights, ensuring that the land can continue to be used for agriculture.The ranch, located near Burns across Eagle and Routt counties, has been in the Nottingham family for decades. Susan's parents, Bill Nottingham Jr. and Neva Snook, spent more than 60 years building the property into one of Colorado's largest working cattle ranches. Their daughter has now taken steps to ensure that the land they assembled is not divided and sold for development.The Colorado Cattlemen's Agricultural Land Trust (CCALT) announced the completion of a conservation easement covering the property. Under this agreement, the ranch will remain privately owned and can continue its agricultural operations, but its future development will be permanently restricted.The decision marks a major change for Nottingham, who had previously considered selling the ranch. According to The Colorado Sun, the property was listed for $100 million in 2017. However, the possibility of buyers dividing the land and selling its water rights made her reconsider what she wanted for the family's property.How the Nottingham family built the ranchThe family's ranching history in Colorado goes back to the late 1800s. Susan's parents married in 1950, and began building their own agricultural business.Their first ranch was located on land that is now part of the EagleVail Golf Course in Avon. Over the following six decades, they acquired additional properties that eventually became the Nottingham Ranch.The family moved its ranching operations as development expanded in the Vail Valley. Bill continued working on the ranch until his death in 2014, while Neva also remained closely connected to the property throughout her life.The ranch currently supports approximately 1,200 cattle and produces around 3,000 tonnes of hay each summer, according to The Colorado Sun.Why Susan Nottingham decided against sellingWhen Nottingham placed the property on the market in 2017, she encountered potential buyers who were interested in dividing the ranch and selling its resources separately.Speaking to The Colorado Sun, she described the experience as painful because prospective buyers did not share her family's attachment to the land.Nottingham had also been sceptical of conservation easements, particularly restrictions on private property rights. However, her views changed after she began working with the Colorado Cattlemen's Agricultural Land Trust, an organisation familiar with the needs of working ranchers.She also considered how selling the property to developers could affect neighbouring ranchers, who might face similar pressure to sell their land.Her decision was ultimately shaped by a desire to protect the family's agricultural legacy and prevent the ranch from being divided.Speaking about her parents' contribution, she said, "They’re the ones that took 64 years of their married life and put this all together."What will happen to the land and its water rights?The conservation agreement protects 18,484 acres, including nearly 9,500 acres in Eagle County. According to CCALT, it is the largest conservation easement in the 23-year history of Eagle County's Open Space Fund.Importantly, the agreement also protects more than 175 cubic feet per second of senior water rights connected to tributaries of the Colorado River.These rights are particularly important because the ranch depends on water for its agricultural operations. The agreement will keep the protected water rights tied to the property.The land also provides habitat for elk, mule deer, bighorn sheep, pronghorn, bald eagles and greater sage-grouse. Its conservation will help protect these habitats alongside the ranch's agricultural activities.The project received support from several organisations, including Great Outdoors Colorado, the National Fish and Wildlife Foundation, the Natural Resources Conservation Service and The Nature Conservancy.You use AI every day. articles.title: Pope Leo XIV to undergo lung surgery ahead of major South America trip in November
articles.summary: Pope Leo XIV is set to undergo surgery in the coming days to remove a small nodule from his lung, which doctors discovered during a recent medical
articles.body: Pope Leo XIV is set to undergo surgery in the coming days to remove a small nodule from his lung, which doctors discovered during a recent medical examination.The Vatican said on Sunday that the procedure was scheduled for the first few days of the week, with the 71-year-old pontiff expected to take about a week to recover.Addressing the public during his traditional Sunday noon blessing, Leo thanked those who had expressed concern and asked them to keep him in their prayers.The pope said the abnormality had been detected at an early stage and was localised, adding that he had decided to proceed with surgery on medical advice.In remarks delivered in Italian, Leo said, “doctors found a small, localized nodule in my lung. It was detected at a very early stage and is circumscribed. The doctors believe it’s best to take action, so, following their advice, I’ve decided to have surgery to remove it."“The surgery is already scheduled for the coming days. Thank you for your spiritual support, and I entrust myself to your prayers,” he said.The pontiff is expected to undergo the procedure at Rome's Gemelli hospital, a facility that has treated several popes, including his predecessor, Pope Francis. The hospital has a dedicated apartment for pontiffs.Leo has no previously known health problems and is regarded as physically active. His routine has included weekly tennis sessions and swimming at the papal summer residence in Castel Gandolfo.The planned surgery comes ahead of a major overseas trip scheduled for November 6 to 17, during which Leo is expected to visit Uruguay, Argentina and Peru. It remains unclear whether the procedure and recovery period will affect his travel plans. However, he indicated during his Sunday remarks that he intended to proceed with the trip.Leo's predecessor, Pope Francis, died on April 21, 2025, following a stroke after a prolonged hospital stay that began with a respiratory crisis and developed into double pneumonia. Francis had suffered from chronic lung disease and had part of one lung removed when he was a young man.You use AI every day. Now get your AI Quotient. Take the AIQ test.

articles.title: Over 100 killed, including 15 children, as Yemen-headed boat capsizes in Red Sea
articles.summary: At least 109 migrants, including 15 children, have died after a Yemen-headed boat carrying over 300 people capsized off the coast of Djibouti in East
articles.body: At least 109 migrants, including 15 children, have died after a Yemen-headed boat carrying over 300 people capsized off the coast of Djibouti in East Africa, the International Organisation for Migration said on Sunday.The boat was travelling from Djibouti to Yemen when it capsized during the night of October 8-9, according to the IOM, which cited survivor accounts. The incident occurred near Guhere, north of Obock, a port town in Djibouti.The fatalities included 52 men, 42 women and 15 children. More than 80 people survived the shipwreck, all of them Ethiopian nationals, Reuters reported, citing a source.At least 116 others remain missing.“This is a devastating loss of life,” said Alexandre Coissac, IOM chief of mission in Djibouti. “This tragedy is a stark reminder of the dangers faced by migrants along this migration corridor as they seek economic opportunities.”Tens of thousands of migrants from the Horn of Africa travel through Djibouti and cross the Bab el-Mandeb Strait towards Gulf countries in search of safety and economic opportunities, the IOM said. The movement has continued despite the violence in Yemen.Humanitarian crisis worsens amid renewed fightingThe tragedy comes as Yemen's humanitarian crisis has “sharply worsened” amid renewed fighting that has displaced more than 200,000 people since early August, according to the United Nations.Mohamed Yahya, assistant secretary-general for humanitarian affairs and deputy emergency relief coordinator, delivered the warning during a UN Security Council briefing.“Today, I must warn the Council that Yemen's humanitarian crisis has sharply worsened. Further inaction will cost lives,” Yahya said.He said escalating fighting over the past two months had forced families already exhausted by more than a decade of conflict to flee their homes. Many displaced families had exhausted their savings, lost their livelihoods and had few options for finding safety, he added.According to Yahya, more than 2,00,000 people have been displaced across Yemen since early August, marking the highest level of new displacement since the 2022 truce.Nearly 4,000 others have crossed the Bab el-Mandeb Strait to seek safety in Djibouti and Somalia, he said.You use AI every day. articles.title: Trumpiana: Trump trail goes boom boom doom doom again!
articles.summary: Wizard of Mar-a-Lago mixes oil and fire to stem the ominous midterm tides Donald Trump hit the campaign trail belching smoke and fire seeming to suggest
articles.body: Wizard of Mar-a-Lago mixes oil and fire to stem the ominous midterm tidesDonald Trump hit the campaign trail belching smoke and fire seeming to suggest Tehran could ‘take out’ Los Angeles and San Diego as he paused plans to attack Iran before the Nov. 3 midterms.“They can take out a city. Let them take – let them take out Los Angeles. Let them take out San Diego,” he boomed at a campaign rally in Nebraska to cheers from the MAGA crowd. “That’s – this is a very small price to pay, and it’s going to be over with very soon.”As California leaders reacted with horror with governor Gavin Newsom calling him “deranged and dangerous,” Trump changed the narrative at another rally in San Antonio, Texas, “We protect our cities. We protect our country. We’re not letting that happen.”“All I was doing was making a comparison between paying a little more, for a short time, for Gasoline, versus the bombing of our Major Cities,” he posted on Truth Social blaming “the Fake and Artificial News Degenerates,” for causing the ‘confusion’ amid ongoing “productive discussions” with Tehran.Then dropping another bomb on European allies, Trump announced a stunning agreement to buy Russian diesel, upending years of U.S. and western pressure on the Kremlin to end its four-and-a-half year war against Ukraine.“Russia will immediately supply over 300,000 Tons of Diesel Fuel to the American and Global Marketplace, another 500,000 Tons during the month of November, and 1,000,000 Tons immediately thereafter,” Trump wrote on Truth Social calling the deal “essential” to reduce fuel prices in the U.S.“Diesel prices for Americans and, indeed, the world, will be COMING DOWN, IN RECORD NUMBERS, AND FAST! Lower prices for Americans, especially our Great Farmers, Ranchers, and Truckers, is my greatest priority,” he wrote.Amid biting criticism from Ukraine’s Zelenskyy, who called it “a happy birthday present for Putin,” and opposition Democrats, Trump turned his guns on another ‘enemy’ — Norway for denying him the Nobel Prize a second time although the Norwegian government doesn’t pick the winner.“We will not forget, Norway,” he fumed at a rally for Republican candidates in Syracuse, New York. “The United States of America, represented by me as your president, should have received the Nobel peace prize, but didn’t.”“And this is an indelible stain on the country of Norway, and those people that made such a disgraceful and embarrassing decision,” Trump said. “The Nobel peace prize has been forever discredited by a handful of radical ideologues who are anti-democracy and really enemies of civilization.”Trump also recited a list of wars he claims to have settled, including an India-Pakistan conflict, saying “I’m about to settle or win two more: Iran and Russia-Ukraine”— very “quickly.”“I will tell you what,” he added, darkly, “Iran will be very quick one way or the other: that they give us everything or they don’t exist any longer.”Despite his “unbelievable accomplishments, the Nobel prize was given out today to a liberal person who works at the United Nations, who nobody has ever heard of,” Trump said of Navi Pillay, the South African former UN human rights chief of Indian origin.But “this woman,” as Trump called the winner, quickly turned the tables on him quipping to an applauding crowd, “If you clap a little bit more, I may share this prize with Trump” — leaving unsaid how Trump had snagged the medal from last year’s winner, Venezuelan opposition leader María Corina Machado.Back in Washington, Trump found yet another enemy. “The White House considers anyone that uses the term, ‘Artificial Intelligence,’ as opposed to the highly accepted new and more accurate term, ‘Super Intelligence,’ THE ENEMY! ” he declared before hosting an awards party for tech billionaires.In a building named the Donald J Trump Institute of Peace in Washington, he dished out awards to six tech leaders and even received an award that belonged to his late “super genius” uncle Dr John Trump, an MIT professor who received the National Medal of Science in 1983.Among five immigrants who received awards at the event celebrating the “golden age” of American innovation was Microsoft chief Satya Nadella from India hours after Vice President JD Vance announced Microsoft’s suspension from a program allowing companies to sponsor foreign workers for green cards.But amid hectic campaigning and burdens of high office, the former real estate mogul did not forget his pet projects. At an event to celebrate Italian explorer Christopher Columbus, he unveiled a 13-foot Columbus statue at the White House.Trump also announced plans to turn his West Palm Beach golf club into a new Camp David-style presidential retreat where presidents could vacation, meet foreign leaders and conduct high-level diplomacy.The plan calls for the federal government to be granted part of the property, with the rest maintained as a private course. The compound would not be for him but for presidents who follow him in office, the POTUS declared magnanimously in the Oval Office.“They asked if I’d be willing to do it, and I said I would be. This wouldn’t be for me. This would be for all future presidents,” he said. Asked whether the retreat would be called “Camp Donald,” Trump reminded it already had a name: Trump International.Meanwhile, as the United States joined a superpower race to put nuclear reactors on the Moon with NASA asking contractors to build one ready for launch by 2030, the White House posted, “America will establish a permanent presence on the moon. ”While some followers suggested sending illegal immigrants or top opposition Democratic leaders there, one enthusiastic fan posted a picture of Trump striding to lead the mission himself saying, “LET’S GO!! ” — and establish his permanent presence there!(By arrangement with The American Bazaar)You use AI every day. articles.summary: COIMBATORE: Saibaba Colony police in the city on Saturday registered a case against a couple on charges of cheating a pawnbroker of Rs 76 lakh by
articles.body: COIMBATORE: Saibaba Colony police in the city on Saturday registered a case against a couple on charges of cheating a pawnbroker of Rs 76 lakh by promising to redeem 710 grams of gold pledged with another finance company and re-pledge it with his firm.The complainant, N Harihara Subramanian, 53 of Vadavalli, runs a jewellery pawnbroking firm on Alagesan Road in Saibaba Colony. He provides financial assistance to people seeking to redeem jewellery pledged with other finance companies, on the assurance that they would re-pledge the ornaments with his firm.According to the complaint, Kesavaraj and his wife Uma Maheswari, residents of Veerakeralam near Vadavalli, approached Subramanian on Sept 30. They told him that they had pledged 710 grams of gold jewellery with another finance company for Rs 76 lakh and sought financial assistance to redeem it.The couple promised to pledge the redeemed jewellery with Subramanian’s firm in return for the money. Trusting their assurance, he transferred Rs 76 lakh to Kesavaraj’s bank account.However, the couple failed to redeem the jewellery and pledge it with his firm. They did not return the money. articles.title: 18-year-old feared drowned while collecting Gangajal in Bhojpur
articles.summary: 18-year-old Abhay Kumar Singh feared drowned in the Ganga at Mahuli Ghat, Bhojpur, while collecting Gangajal for Navratri; SDRF search ongoing.
articles.body: Ara: An 18-year-old boy was feared drowned in Ganga after he slipped into deep water while collecting Gangajal and sacred soil for Kalash Sthapana on the first day of Navratri at Mahuli Ganga Ghat under Sinha police station area in Bhojpur district on Sunday morning. His elder sister, who jumped into the river in an attempt to save him, was rescued by local boatmen.The boy, identified as Abhay Kumar Singh, son of Hemant Kumar Singh of Gheghata village under Ara Mufassil police station, had gone to the ghat under Sinha police station in Barhara block with his sisters, Nikki and Nitisha, on a motorcycle.SHO Raju Kumar said State Disaster Response Force (SDRF) launched a search after police were informed about the incident, but Abhay could not be traced till late Sunday afternoon. “Though the SDRF personnel have been searching for the boy since morning, his body has not been found till late Sunday afternoon,” the SHO told TOI.The SHO said police initially received two versions of the incident, with some reports suggesting that Abhay drowned while trying to save his sister. However, subsequent inquiries indicated that Abhay had ventured into deeper water to collect Ganga jal and take a holy dip when he slipped.His elder sister Nikki jumped into the river in an attempt to save him but could not reach him. She was subsequently rescued by local boatmen from the shallower part of the river, police said.Abhay’s uncle Rajendra Singh said the incident occurred around 7 am. “Abhay had come here on his bike with his sisters to fetch Ganga jal and take a holy dip, but he accidentally slipped and drowned,” he said.praveensibu@gmail.comYou Can Also Check: Gold Rate in Patna | Silver Rate in Patna | Bank Holidays in Patna | Public Holidays in Patna | Patna AQI | Weather in Patna | Petrol Price in Patna | Diesel Price in Patna | CNG Price in Patna | LPG Price in PatnaStay updated with the latest Patna news.
